summary: Describes what IPsec and IKE need to do to protect SCTP traffic, since SCTP can use several addresses for one connection. It lists functional requirements. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: SCTP can use more than one road at a time. This memo says what the lock-and-key system for network traffic must do to protect all of them.

questions: how does sctp work with ipsec
what is the ike id_list number
subtitle: What IPsec and IKE must do so that SCTP associations with several addresses can be protected.

tldr.problem: SCTP lets one association use several source and destination addresses, but IPsec and IKE were built around one address pair per connection.
tldr.mechanism: SCTP traffic is treated as ordinary IPsec traffic, with address sets in the policy and SA databases and a new IKE identity type, ID_LIST, that can carry many identities at once.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can protect a multi-address SCTP association without one SA pair per address combination, provided every address is validated against the peer's authority.

facts.label: SA identifier
facts.value: ({set of destination addresses}, SPI, Security Protocol)

today: RFC 3554 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a requirements document for IPsec and IKE as they existed in 2003 (RFC 2401 and RFC 2409).

sections.title: Why SCTP Needs Extra IPsec Rules
sections.content:
The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) is a reliable transport protocol that runs on a connection-less packet network such as IP. It was designed to carry PSTN signaling messages over IP networks, but it can be used more broadly.

SCTP may use IPsec (the Authentication Header and the Encapsulating Security Payload) for integrity and confidentiality, and a key negotiation protocol such as IKE to set up IPsec Security Associations (SAs). This document gives functional requirements for IPsec and IKE so they work well with SCTP. The two changes it discusses are a new ID type in IKE and implementation choices in IPsec processing, both needed because one SCTP association can have many source and destination addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP can use many addresses at once, like a family with several phone numbers. The old security rules only expected one number, so this memo adds the missing pieces.

sections.title: SCTP Inside IPsec
sections.content:
When AH or ESP protects SCTP, the SCTP frame is treated as just another transport layer protocol on top of IP, like TCP or UDP. IPsec implementations should already be able to use the IANA-assigned SCTP protocol number as a selector in the Security Policy Database (SPD). Using the SCTP source and destination ports as selectors is described as straightforward, but the IPsec code that finds the ports has to be modified because a port's location in the header is protocol specific.

That is not enough, because SCTP can negotiate sets of source and destination addresses, not necessarily in the same subnet or address range. One SPD entry per address pair works but is expensive. The better approach is to attach sets of addresses to the source and destination selectors of each SPD entry. For non-SCTP traffic those sets hold one element. This is an implementation decision, but implementors are encouraged to follow it.

SAs likewise can have several addresses. An SA is identified by the extended triplet ({set of destination addresses}, SPI, Security Protocol). A lookup in the Security Association Database (SADB) with (Destination Address, SPI, Security Protocol), where the destination is any of the negotiated peer addresses, MUST return the same SA.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of writing a separate rule for every pair of addresses, you keep one rule with a list of addresses. Whichever address on the list you look up, you find the same rule.

sections.title: Negotiating Many Addresses in IKE Phase 2
sections.content:
IKE MUST be able to negotiate multiple addresses efficiently in Phase 2 (Quick Mode). Negotiating one pair of IPsec SAs for every combination of addresses works, and all current IKE implementations support it, but it can create an unnecessarily large number of SAs and waste time and memory.

The RFC therefore defines a new identity type, ID_LIST, which allows recursive inclusion of IDs. The Phase 2 Initiator ID for an SCTP association MAY be an ID_LIST containing as many ID_IPV4_ADDR IDs as needed, and the same goes for Responder IDs. Implementations MUST support this type. Other selector types MAY still be used when each peer uses only one address.

Rules for the new type:

  • An ID_LIST cannot appear inside another ID_LIST. Any ID type from RFC 2407 can be included, and each contained ID carries a complete Identification Payload header.
  • The Next Payload field of the included IDs MUST be ignored by the Responder. The Protocol ID and Port fields of the ID_LIST payload itself are set to zero by the Initiator and MUST be ignored by the Responder.
  • Different ID types, such as an ID_FQDN and an ID_IPV4_ADDR, can be mixed. If any included type is invalid in the context, the whole list is at fault and the Responder should signal a fault and stop processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of showing the guard one ID card at a time, you hand over a folder holding all the cards. If one card in the folder is no good, the guard rejects the whole folder.

sections.title: Validating Identities in Phase 1
sections.content:
For IKE to validate the Phase 2 selectors, enough information must be exchanged in Phase 1. IKE already handles the simple case of two peers by using Phase 1 IDs that match their IP addresses and putting the same addresses in the SubjAltName of the certificates. For more complicated cases, external policy or another mechanism must be consulted. All addresses presented in Phase 2 selectors MUST be validated, using evidence from the Phase 1 certificates if possible, or out-of-band means such as administrator-configured policy.

To support the simple scenario with several addresses, it MUST be possible to specify multiple Phase 1 IDs (the ID_LIST method can be reused) and to authenticate them. With pre-shared keys, the same key is associated with all acceptable peer IDs. With certificates there are two options:

  • One certificate holding several IDs in SubjAltName as an ASN.1 sequence. This is the preferred solution and conformant implementations MUST support it.
  • Several certificates in multiple CERT payloads. Implementations MAY support this. Only one signature is issued per Phase 1 exchange, so all certificates must have the same key as their Subject, and the RFC says it offers no significant advantage over the first option.

Either way, the IKE implementation must verify each claimed Phase 1 ID.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone says they own several addresses, the guard has to check each claim. A single badge that lists all the addresses is the neatest proof.

sections.title: Changing Addresses and Fixing the Selector Offer
sections.content:
SCTP does not currently support changing the addresses of an association while it is in use, though it may in the future. Unless the set changes extremely often, a full Phase 1 and Phase 2 exchange is enough to set up the right selectors and SAs.

A second issue is the initial offer. Under IKE, the Responder echoes in the second Quick Mode message the IDs it received in the first, so the Initiator is assumed to know every selector. In most cases the Responder knows its own addresses better, so the selectors may be insufficient or inaccurate.

If the Responder finds the proposed selectors wrong, it can start a new Quick Mode exchange with the roles reversed. The new Initiator MUST copy the SA and selectors from the old Quick Mode message and change its set of selectors to match reality. All SCTP-supporting IKE implementations MUST be able to do this.
sections.plainLanguage: If you tell your friend the wrong list of your phone numbers, they can call you back and correct the list. That second call is the new Quick Mode exchange.

sections.title: Redirection Attacks and Address Authority
sections.content:
SCTP's support for mobility opens up traffic-redirection attacks. An attacker X claims that X's address should be added to an SCTP session between peers A and B and used for later communication, so traffic between A and B can be seen by X. If X is not on the path between A and B, SCTP gives X attack capabilities it would not otherwise have. All such address updates should therefore be authenticated.

Since IKE negotiates the IPsec SAs for these sessions, IKE MUST validate all addresses attached to an SCTP endpoint, either through the certificates presented in Phase 1 or through an out-of-band method. In Phase 2, the Responder MUST verify that the Initiator is authorized to receive traffic for every address in its selectors. Otherwise any valid peer of the Responder could see another valid peer's traffic just by claiming its address.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky person might say 'send my friend's mail to my house too.' So the post office must check that you really own every address you ask for.

sections.title: The ID_LIST Number
sections.content: IANA has assigned the number 12 to ID_LIST in the "IPSEC Identification Type" registry, which is part of the ISAKMP Identifiers table. The type itself is defined in section 3 of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Every kind of ID card gets a number. The new folder-of-cards type was given the number 12.
